title: The Read-for-15 Challenge
intro: Text 1 is a poster for a reading challenge run by a neighbourhood library.

visual.text: YOUR NEIGHBOURHOOD LIBRARY · JUNE HOLIDAY CHALLENGE
You have fifteen minutes. You just spent them on someone else’s holiday photos.
The Read-for-15 Challenge: one small slice of your day, any book you like.
A teenager sits on a bench at an MRT platform with a paperback open on his knees, so absorbed that he has not noticed the train doors opening behind him. His phone lies face down beside him.

Nobody is asking you to finish a classic by Friday. Fifteen minutes is the bus ride home, the queue for bubble tea, the wait while your rice cools. Read a comic, a cookbook, a football biography — it all counts. Do it for twenty-one days and see whether you can still stop.

visual.title: How to join
items: Pick up a bookmark tracker at the counter
Colour one square for every day you read for fifteen minutes
Return a full bookmark by 30 June for a lucky draw — and keep the habit for free

visual.text: “I started with one volume of manga on Day 1. By Day 21 I was halfway through a thick mystery and annoyed when my stop came.” — Marcus, 14
Stuck for ideas? Ask any librarian for the ‘If you liked that, try this’ shelf.
Start today. Day 1 is the hardest.

text2.intro: Text 2 is taken from a blog post by a fifteen-year-old about her June holidays.
paragraphs: I signed up for the library’s reading challenge mainly for the lucky draw. On the first day, I set a timer on my phone, opened a cookbook my mother had left on the table and stared at a recipe for kueh lapis until the alarm rang. It felt like homework.

By the end of the first week, though, something had changed. I stopped setting the timer, because I kept reading past it anyway. I read on the bus, in the clinic waiting room, even in the queue at the bubble tea shop. My brother laughed at me, then quietly borrowed the mystery I had just finished.
I did not win the lucky draw, and I honestly did not mind.

Look at the picture in Text 1. Say what it shows, and explain how it supports the headline ‘You have fifteen minutes. You just spent them on someone else’s holiday photos.’

scheme.answer: The boy is so absorbed in his book, with his phone face down, that he does not notice the train doors opening [1]; this backs the headline’s point that spare minutes are better spent reading than scrolling through a phone [1].
points: What it shows: the teenager is lost in his book, with his phone face down beside him / he does not notice the train doors opening.
How it backs the words: a few spare minutes, such as waiting for a train, can go to reading instead of the phone.

seeds.text: The boy is so into his book that he does not even see the train doors open, and his phone is face down. This supports the headline because it shows that the short waiting time can be used for reading instead of looking at other people’s photos on the phone.
His phone is turned over and he is busy reading at the MRT, so it shows that instead of scrolling social media in the few minutes you have, you can read and enjoy it.
The boy is reading so hard that he does not notice the train doors opening behind him.
It tells readers to use their waiting time to read a book instead of scrolling on their phones.
It shows that teenagers should not take the MRT alone.
The picture is interesting and catches the reader’s eye.
